scene.testo: Imagine you are floating inside a metal can the size of a small closet at 6 AM, strapped into a sleeping bag on the wall. The ship is roaring around Earth at 17,500 mph. You have not slept well in days.

The first humans to leave Earth did not get a luxury hotel. They got cramped capsules, tubes of food, and a toilet problem nobody had solved. This is what daily life was really like for the first astronauts.

On April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin circled Earth once in 108 minutes. On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard flew for just 15 minutes. Those short trips opened a door, and every later mission had to answer one question: how do humans live up there?

Start with the room. The Mercury capsule was so small that astronauts joked you did not climb into it, you wore it. NASA describes the cabin as barely larger than a phone booth, and that was home for hours.
On February 20, 1962, John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth. He circled three times in about 4 hours and 55 minutes. He was strapped in tight and could barely move the whole time.

Glenn was also the first American to eat in space. His food came in aluminum tubes, like toothpaste. He squeezed applesauce into his mouth, and NASA wanted to know one thing: can a human swallow in weightlessness?

The answer was yes. Swallowing works fine without gravity. That small test mattered, because doctors had worried food might simply refuse to go down. Instead, the applesauce went down, and the worry went away.

But early space food was not exactly a feast. Astronauts ate bite-sized cubes, freeze-dried powders, and pastes. The cubes crumbled, and crumbs are dangerous in zero gravity, because they float into your eyes and your equipment.

Gemini astronauts often rehydrated meals by squirting water into a plastic bag, waiting, then squeezing the food out through a tube. Some of them said the food tasted bland. Many crews ate less than doctors wanted.
Then came Apollo, and the menu got better. By the Apollo missions, crews could add hot water to meals and eat with a spoon. Some packages were made so the food stuck to the spoon like glue.

Now for the question every kid asks. How do you use the bathroom in a capsule? For the first flights, the answer was almost nothing. On Shepard's 15-minute flight in 1961, the plan did not include a way to go.
Shepard waited on the launch pad for hours, and the flight was delayed. By his own account, he finally had to go inside his spacesuit. Doctors then had to turn off some of the sensors on his body.

After that, engineers made a fix. Astronauts wore a urine collection device, a kind of bag attached to the body. For solid waste, they used sticky plastic bags taped to the skin. It was awkward and messy.

Crews on Apollo later described the process as one of the worst parts of the trip. It could take up to an hour, and the smell stayed in the cabin. In a spacecraft that small, you cannot open a window.
Next, sleep. In a spacecraft going 17,500 mph, the sun rises and sets about every 90 minutes. That means about 16 sunrises every 24 hours, and the light keeps hitting your window.
Gemini 7 in December 1965 was the longest flight of its time, nearly 14 days. Frank Borman and Jim Lovell lived in a cabin about the size of the front seat of a car. They slept in shifts, curled up.
Borman later said he and Lovell wore their suits for much of the mission. For the second week, they were allowed to take the suits off, one man at a time. Even then, they could barely stretch out.
Apollo gave crews a little more room. The command module held three men in a cone about 11 feet wide at the base. Imagine three grown men living for a week in a space smaller than a minivan.

Apollo crews often slept in hammock-style sleeping bags hung inside the cabin. In weightlessness, you float, so the bag is there to keep you from drifting into a switch. Astronauts also wore masks over their eyes.
Even so, rest was hard. Apollo 8 astronauts in December 1968 reported poor sleep. Noise from pumps and fans never stopped. The cabin was cold, and the astronauts sometimes had to wake up for tasks.

Temperature mattered, too. Outside a spacecraft in sunlight, it can reach about +250°F. In shadow, it can drop to -250°F. That is a swing of 500 degrees, and the walls of the capsule were all that stood between.
To stay balanced, Apollo spacecraft slowly rotated, like a chicken on a rotisserie. NASA called it passive thermal control. Rolling about once an hour spread the heat so no side baked and none froze.

Inside, cabin temperatures usually stayed in a comfortable range, but not always. Apollo 13 astronauts in April 1970 suffered when the spacecraft lost power. The cabin dropped to near 40 degrees Fahrenheit.

The crew wore what they had. They were cold, thirsty, and exhausted. They had cut their water rations, and one astronaut lost about 14 pounds, NASA reports. They still made it home safely on April 17, 1970.

Another problem was your body. In weightlessness, fluids shift toward the head, so many astronauts felt a stuffy face. Some also got space sickness, with nausea and vomiting, during the first days of a mission.

Apollo 8 crew member Frank Borman became sick on the way to the moon, with vomiting and diarrhea. NASA had to think hard about whether space sickness could threaten a mission, and it studied the problem for years.

Over longer flights, the effects grew. Muscles weaken without gravity to push against. Bones lose minerals. After the Skylab missions in 1973 and 1974, doctors measured the loss, and it became a major concern.
Skylab was America's first space station, launched on May 14, 1973. It was about 85 feet long, roughly the length of eight school buses lined up? No, closer to two school buses end to end.
Inside, astronauts finally had room to move. The main workshop was tall enough to float from one end to the other. Crews said it felt like a flying house after the tiny capsules they had known.
Skylab also had a real shower. The crew pulled a cylinder of fabric up around their body, sprayed warm water, and sucked the droplets away with a vacuum. It took about 2 hours to set up and clean.

A Skylab meal was another upgrade. The station had a table, and crews could sit, or at least strap their feet in. Foods included steak, ice cream, and canned items. Meals felt like a real break in the day.

Work, however, was relentless. Skylab crews put in long days, and they fell behind. According to NASA accounts, the third crew in 1973 and 1974 felt pushed too hard, and mission control adjusted the schedule.

Exercise became part of the job. Astronauts rode a stationary bike and used a treadmill-style device. Their reward was less muscle loss, and doctors proved it. Crews who exercised more returned in better shape.
Now imagine the view. Every orbit gives you a window on a planet. Astronauts often said that seeing Earth as a small blue sphere changed how they thought about everything back home.

On Apollo 8, Christmas Eve 1968, three astronauts read from the Book of Genesis while orbiting the moon. Millions of people listened. They had traveled about 240,000 miles, and they were looking back at home.
That same trip took a famous photograph, Earthrise. A blue and white planet hung over a gray lunar horizon. For many people, it became a symbol. It showed Earth as a small, fragile place.

Of course, the most dangerous part was getting home. Reentry slams a capsule into the atmosphere at about 25,000 mph. The heat shield glows, and outside temperatures reach roughly 5,000°F, hotter than molten lava.

During reentry, a blackout cuts radio contact for several minutes. In Apollo missions, mission control waited in silence. Inside the capsule, astronauts felt up to about 6 times their normal weight pressing on their chests.

Then the parachutes opened, and the capsule dropped into the ocean. Splashdown was rough. The capsule bobbed in the waves, and some astronauts felt seasick while they waited for Navy helicopters and divers.

After the first moon landing in July 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts were put in quarantine. They stayed inside a sealed trailer for about 21 days. NASA worried about unknown moon germs, so even heroes waited behind glass.
President Richard Nixon visited them there on July 24, 1969. He spoke through a window. The astronauts stood in their flight suits, smiling, and their families could not hug them yet.

Back on Earth, gravity hit hard. After long flights, astronauts often felt dizzy and heavy. Their legs felt weak, and simple tasks like standing took effort. Doctors checked them closely in the days after landing.
Compare that with your own morning. You wake in a bed, walk to a bathroom, and eat breakfast at a table. For the first astronauts, every one of those simple acts was a problem engineers had to solve.

Those problems did not stay unsolved. Every flight taught NASA something. Better food, better toilets, better beds, and better exercise all came from those early missions. Today's station crews inherit that work.

So what was life really like for the first astronauts? Cramped, cold, noisy, and smelly, with food from tubes and sleep in short pieces. Yet they did it, and every comfort in orbit today began with them.

Here is the most surprising detail. Glenn's first meal in orbit was applesauce from a tube, because doctors truly did not know if humans could swallow in space. A pasty snack settled a question about the whole future.
If you could spend one day in a capsule, would you do it? Tell me in the comments. And if you want more stories from space history, subscribe to Orbital Days. See you in the next one.

What was life really like for the first astronauts? Go inside the tiny Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo capsules and the Skylab station to see how early space travelers ate, slept, used the toilet, and survived the trip home. From John Glenn's applesauce in 1962 to the Apollo 13 crew freezing in April 1970, every detail here comes from documented missions. We also note where the record is uncertain.
